title: CEO Fraud in 2026: How It Works, Examples & Prevention
summary: CEO fraud in 2026: how deepfake and email scams work, real cases, red flags, and the verification process that stops them.
body_markdown:
## CEO fraud examples: four recent cases and one classic


These CEO fraud examples, dating from 2015–2025, show the complexity of more recent cases and how quickly CEO fraud has evolved.


### Example #1: Multinational company (Singapore)


**Date:** March 2025


**What happened** : The finance director of an unnamed multinational company was messaged on WhatsApp by someone posing as the CFO. They spoke to a fake lawyer and joined a Zoom call with deepfaked executives, including the CEO. They then transferred nearly US$500,000. Luckily, Singapore and Hong Kong police[traced and withheld the funds within days](https://www.police.gov.sg/media-hub/news/2025/04/20250407_singapore_and_hong_kong_police_force_recover_over_%24670000_in_a_scam) .


**Outcome:** Nearly US$500,000 fully recovered


### Example #2: Ferrari (Italy)


**Date:** July 2024


**What happened:** A Ferrari executive received a[WhatsApp message from someone impersonating CEO Benedetto Vigna](https://fortune.com/europe/2024/07/27/ferrari-deepfake-attempt-scammer-security-question-ceo-benedetto-vigna-cybersecurity-ai/) – using an unfamiliar number – about a confidential and highly sensitive deal. When the fake Vigna then called to discuss the deal, the executive noticed a slight stiffness in his voice, which prompted him to ask something only the *real* Vigna would know: what was the book he had recommended to the executive recently? Unable to answer, the scammer hung up.


**Outcome:** Failed attempt


### Example #3: WPP (United Kingdom)


**Date:** May 2024


**What happened:** The Guardian reported that[WPP CEO Mark Read](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/article/2024/may/10/ceo-wpp-deepfake-scam) was impersonated using an elaborate deepfake attempt on a Microsoft Teams call. Criminals impersonated Read using a fake WhatsApp account, a voice clone, and YouTube footage, trying to persuade an agency executive to set up a new business and hand over money and personal details.


**Outcome:** Failed attempt


### Example #4: Arup (Hong Kong)


**Date:** January 2024


**What happened:** A finance employee at[Arup](https://www.weforum.org/stories/emerging-technologies/deepfake-ai-cybercrime-arup) joined a video call in which he thought he was chatting to his CFO and other finance colleagues to discuss a sensitive deal – but everyone in the meeting was being impersonated by sophisticated video deepfakes.


**Outcome:** Approximately US$25 million lost


### Example #5: Ubiquiti Networks (United States)


**Date: June** 2015


**What happened:** Scammers impersonated Ubiquiti Networks staff and sent fraudulent payment requests to the finance department, prompting the company’s Hong Kong subsidiary to wire about $46.7 million to overseas accounts held by third parties. Ubiquiti recovered about $15 million and was still trying to recover the remaining $31.7 million.


**Outcome:**[US$46.7 million lost](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/security/ubiquiti-networks-says-it-was-victim-47-million-cyber-scam-n406201) , approximately US$15 million recovered


As these five examples show, there’s no end to the creativity and inventiveness scammers demonstrate when targeting us with CEO fraud. And while we might occasionally get lucky – like the quick-witted Ferrari executive – we can’t rely on luck to stay safe.
